These graphs have the unique property that no two points are equivalent in terms of their distances to other points. It's proven that in these graphs, the identifying set consists of the fewest points when compared to other identifying sets, and we've found the minimum size of these identifying sets for trees with this property. Additionally, we've found the minimum size of these identifying sets for certain other classes of graphs.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of residence time and reactor size on SO2 removal. Ultimately, under optimized conditions, the results show that an ozone-UV light system can be a suitable solution for sustainable air pollution control applications.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. To address this, researchers have developed a simulation framework using C++ that leverages the capabilities of multi-core processors, allowing for efficient testing of large-scale neuromorphic engineering designs on modern computers. This proof-of-concept approach has shown significant speed improvements, with particular benefits noticed in simulations involving millions of neurons and extended run times. We outline the core algorithms used in the simulator and present results from testing various configurations, highlighting the advantages of multi-core simulation for neuromorphic computing.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems.

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated bounds unnecessary.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve educational tools by providing various forms of feedback that not only point out errors but also guide students towards best practices in testing. Three distinct types of feedback - explanation, redirection, and positive guidance - are incorporated into Rentier, an interactive testing environment that works closely with students to perform a task. By contrast to the traditional "point-and-click" style of most educational tools, Rentier showcases the teacher-student interaction as a collaborative process. By incorporating feedback and involving students in the testing process through a series of questions and guidance, Rentier empowers students to develop effective testing skills and provides them with a solid foundation to succeed in professional testing environments.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive, descriptive verbal explanation of a DNN's decision rationale through an analysis of learned features, associated human-interpretable concepts, and an ILP approach resulting in logical rules that faithfully mirror the behavior of the original complex model. The implementation details are made publicly accessible on GitHub.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various strategies to mitigate it.

Dark matter particle research has been conducted using a dataset of Z boson candidates accompanied by a significant amount of undetected energy produced by proton-proton collisions. Data was collected between 2016 and 2018 at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV using the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, equating to 137 fb^-1 of accumulated luminosity. By examining two distinct particle decays – one involving electron pairs and the other muon pairs – researchers have found no evidence to support the standard model's predictions. Instead, this analysis provides a comprehensive statistical assessment of the likelihood that dark matter particles may exist.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage can be adjusted through adjustment of the graphene's surface terraine. It's suggested that an interface disorder and epitaxial interaction between GdPtSb and the defective graphene surface leads to the creation of a disordered and changeable interface potential, causing the auto-rotation of the GdPtSb crystal structure. Moreover, this investigation has shown that this rotation domain can be completely eliminated in higher lattice-mismatch Heusler compounds such as LaPtSb. This research is the first to provide experimental evidence of a remote epitaxy process and could pave the way for remote epitaxy's widespread application.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of economic data, even when individual observations are rare and noisy. A new method allows us to make this analysis by looking at the first few eigenvalues of a variance-covariance matrix, which can be estimated from these data. This method works by assuming that key patterns in these data are consistent over time, which is the case even if randomness affects these patterns. As a result, we can confidently detect the first few patterns in these data, even if their rarity makes it difficult to do so. This method also works well when data are sampled infrequently, such as annually. Its applications are diverse, covering the analysis of time series, cross-sectional data, and mixed datasets. Which trends to focus on depends on whether they rise or fall: We can focus on trends that rise over time, on trends that fall over time, or on trends that are consistent across observations. Our approach is versatile and works well with data that are sampled at different frequencies, even with missing values. Its ease of use also makes it accessible to analysts who are new to stochastic trend analysis.

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo, the massive galaxy cluster, have identified 23 known groups of multiply distorted galaxy images and 8 previously undiscovered ones, all verified spectroscopically by MUSE. By analyzing these groups, researchers created a lens model which allowed them to locate 37 more groups, comprising 28 new and 9 previously identified systems. Based on the initial lens model, researchers estimated the ages of 37 new groups. Furthermore, a more refined lens model revealed 37 more multiply distorted galaxy images and allowed for a more precise estimation of the ages of 21 of these groups. Through the process of image deconvolution, researchers constructed the most detailed map of El Gordo's mass distribution to date, which provided insights into the distribution of dark matter and gravitational force. By using the refined lens model, researchers identified 84 likely galaxy images and further improved the accuracy of the ages of 37 groups. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of the ages and star formation rates of galaxies at different positions in the cluster revealed no clear difference and, thus, no evidence of significant impact of environmental factors on galaxy evolution.

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a Nash Bargaining model, resulting in improved outcomes for all parties.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract derivation also enables the definition of a natural geometric framework for understanding the algebra's underlying structure.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of upcoming cosmological observations, also having connections to supergravity. Exponential and polynomial models of this type are compared against recent data from the field (notably Planck 2018 plus LWA "LowB" dataset), with a discussion on the model's predictive capabilities and potential shortcomings, along with an examination of the model space's likelihood under different data inputs. The assessment of the model's goodness of fit is done via two metrics: discrepancy and information-criticality. It appears that polynomial $\alpha$-attractors are more compatible with the Planck 2018 data than similar exponential models, although both fall short in a statistical sense.

In this study, we examine a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold, denoted as $X$, and its associated boundary $\partial X$, which is an unoriented two-dimensional surface. We assume that $\partial X$ contains at least three distinct foliations. Our research offers a novel observation: there exists a measured foliation $F$ on $\partial X$ such that its horizontal tangent space effectively covers the surface while ensuring that the horizontal tangent space to $\partial X$ remains well-defined in the vicinity of its boundary except at three distinct points where the foliation is leafwise convergent.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function at any given time. Specifically, we define key parameters such as the mean, variance, and cumulative distribution function of a portfolio's returns, and develop algorithms for interpolation, extrapolation, and forecasting based on historical data. Our results demonstrate how geometric techniques and splines can significantly improve the efficiency of these computations compared to conventional methods.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by non-reliable recording devices.  Research utilizing real-world clinical environments has primarily focused on recording techniques rather than addressing the inherent issues of unreliable recording technology.  To fill this gap, our study features a dataset collected using four distinct recording methods to capture three types of cardiac auscultation sounds in a real-world setting.  Since all four recording methods have inherent flaws, as well as their own strengths and weaknesses, this dataset enables the development of robust algorithms for auscultation analysis.  Our research showcases recording samples collected from an actual clinical environment, followed by an evaluation of their implications for creating effective algorithms.  By distributing this dataset, our goal is to promote research in this field and contribute to the advancement of accurate abnormality detection of heart conditions through recording technology enhancement.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, whereas other calculations relied on sum-over-states methods. Additionally, we addressed concerns about the estimated uncertainty in our study.

A twist is utilized as a localized element in the study of topological K-theory. 
Within the framework of equivariant analysis, twists are categorized into four distinct forms, which can be visualized geometrically. 
This paper examines all possible forms of twists for a torus with actions imposed by 2D space groups, and equivalently, all finite subgroups in the torus's mapping class group. 
The study employs calculations involving Borel's equivariant cohomology and the Leray-Serre spectral sequence to achieve its goals. 
As an additional outcome, the equivariant cohomology up to the third degree is found in all instances, and connections are also drawn with twists related to Freed-Moore K-theory.

Pomona College's Mathematics & Statistics Department has been dedicated to
establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. To achieve this goal, the department has been
working to implement a more effective admissions policy. Initially, the
department attempted to'remediate' the issue by providing additional math
courses for students who were not well-prepared, but ultimately realized that
this approach did not address the underlying issue. A more successful strategy
involved adopting an anti-deficit approach, which involved modifying the math
curriculum to make it more accessible to students from diverse backgrounds.
However, the department soon recognized that there was another challenge to
inclusive learning - the traditional math curriculum itself. To further
enhance an inclusive learning environment, the department made a significant
effort to reform its curriculum by adopting more inclusive and
mathematics-rich content. This reform not only created opportunities for
students to explore real-world problems but also helped in promoting diversity
within the student body through targeted outreach efforts. A more detailed
account of our experiences and lessons learned will be presented in a forthcoming
publication.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional series operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form $(T_{\gamma}b)(j)$, in the context of $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $\ell^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, a counter-example demonstrates that the operator $T_{\gamma}$ does not yield a bounded mapping from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ serves as a key source of gravity. To study the universe's evolution, we establish a model based on a specific type of spacetime with both rotation and anisotropy and then derive equations governing the model's behavior. By analyzing energy density, the energy parameters, and the equation of state parameter, we find that this theoretical model exhibits spatial anisotropy during the universe's initial development but ultimately undergoes isotropization and features a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime, ultimately leading to a universe with both late-time and early-time isotropization.

We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this ideal is generated by a combination of elements from the Weyl group and specific elementary generators, achieving a complete description of its algebraic structure.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study.

We have developed a novel, highly efficient method for determining the value of $\epsilon_K$, a crucial parameter in the CP-violation Kaon decay analysis, by incorporating data from $K^0_S$ and $\pi^0$ decays. This new approach significantly boosts the sensitivity to $\epsilon_K$ compared to previous methods, without introducing significant biases. We have initially evaluated our technique's potential with the data expected from the NA62 and NA64e experiments, assuming the assumption of CP conservation holds true. Our results indicate that with data from NA62, we can achieve a precision of $\pm 1.3 \times 10^{-18}$ on $\epsilon_K$, while data from NA64e can reach a precision of $\pm 0.7 \times 10^{-18}$. We have also demonstrated that our method is adaptable to potential modifications of the Kaon mixing mechanism.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other datasets and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these questions by as much as 33.9 points. We anticipate the QASPER dataset to drive significant advancements in the field.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the likelihood of a supernova explosion and properties of the matter interface between the proto-neutron star and the surrounding matter play a crucial role in determining neutrino instabilities.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, our study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, we trained and tested a ROI-based CNN model with ROI information derived from infantile ADHD patients and combined training and testing sets. Our results revealed that the model's performance was enhanced when utilizing just 113 critical ROIs instead of the entire brain, with precision and F1-score values of 0.81 and 0.80, respectively, for training, and 0.85 and 0.83, respectively, for testing. This study's findings indicate that utilizing a subset of crucial brain regions for ADHD diagnosis through deep learning can lead to improved model outcomes and efficiency.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present novel approaches, prompting the development of the present study, which presents an innovative, data-driven methodology for acronym identification and disambiguation. By synthesizing the strengths of multiple data-driven models, including RNN-based models and linear models, the proposed method offers superior performance over its component wisdom, and its efficacy is showcased through experimental evaluation on a dataset derived from the Wikipedia corpus.

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of PCR primer pairs that can define objects, there are numerous primer pairs that can initiate additional storage segments, enabling flexible construction of our DNA-storage system. Furthermore, by developing a linear scalability algorithm, we can dynamically expand storage segments as needed. Additionally, by developing a data indexing method, we can enhance data localization and reduce the amount of DNA needed to store our data, ultimately allowing for more efficient data retrieval. Through simulation, we've verified the effectiveness of our proposed segmentation and indexing techniques.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, often initiated by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity, focusing specifically on singular perturbation and phase reduction techniques in the context of two distinct types of oscillators, one built on bistability and the other featuring time delay in negative feedback mechanisms. We examine how temporal separation of oscillatory scales can impact resulting wave speeds and assess the influence of pacemaker size and oscillation frequency. Our analytical findings are further validated by numerical simulations described previously, which were designed to model this phenomenon.

A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These improvements are more efficient than previously known quantum approaches, and for certain values of $\gamma$ and $\eta$, surpass the best classical methods. The upper bounds are matched by lower bounds, and the simplicity of the algorithms will likely endure as better algorithms are devised.

Implementing and effectively using effective AI programs requires substantial data
for testing and validation purposes; thus, a significant need exists for enhancing
data quality to support machine learning processes.  We present a novel approach
using reflective capacities of Java objects to embed contextual information within
objects for the purpose of augmenting data sets.  This methodology is part of
the JDataView library, an open-source data manipulation framework that provides
a unified method for working with diverse data sources.  We outline the benefits
of using this embedded metadata in data management applications and evaluate the
performance of JDataView through a series of benchmark tests.

Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly costly due to the necessity for medical staff to review and confirm the accuracy of the proposed coding. This study presents an innovative method to overcome this challenge by utilizing the structure of a medical thesaurus to automatically suggest potential ICD codes for annotated CTNs. An interesting aspect of this work involves handling the inherent subjectivity and variability present in medical terminology. This approach was tested using the access to a medical database of Japanese patients and has achieved promising results, suggesting its potential for real-world application in clinical settings. Additionally, this study explores the underlying mechanics of this method through an experiment that examines the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm when presented with different levels of annotated data, a factor that is often scarce in the field of medical informatics.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to data sparsity. However, this advantage comes at the cost of decreased algorithm resilience to noise and limited data size. We observe that noise has a more substantial impact on clustering than classification, highlighting potential applications in data analysis where accuracy is paramount.

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, revealing 24 total discoveries or recoveries - ten previously unpublished planets with definitive or probable planetary nature: KMT-2018-BLG-2004, OGLE-2018-BLG-1126, and seven other identified planets; combined with four AnomalyFinder-confirmed new planets from published data, and twelve discovered by visual examination. Together, a study detailing sub-prime planet findings is set to complement our findings. Using the method outlined by Hwang et al. (2022), a modification is introduced to their formalism to remove close/wide and inner/outer degeneracies discrepancies.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to establish direct connections between input images and underlying scene characteristics. However, traditional differentiable renderers are designed to work effectively when camera views align with a standard, upright perspective. This limitation is particularly restrictive when applied to real-world scenes captured by autonomous vehicles or unstructured cameras. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel and efficient differentiable renderer that is adapted to handle misaligned camera views. This renderer is based on a novel parametrization technique that allows the transformation of scene surfaces into general camera coordinates. This has been achieved through the introduction of an early stage renderer module, called the standardization module, that normalizes camera coordinates and a new parametrization technique called the $K_{cam}$-based surface point parametrization. This innovative parametrization technique not only simplifies the complex transformation between arbitrary camera coordinates and scene surfaces but also introduces a low-dimensional encoding of point coordinates. By employing this differentiable renderer, we have established a unified framework for monocular 3D object reconstruction that does not require the alignment of camera views. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of this renderer in successfully reconstructing three-dimensional objects even from strongly misaligned camera views.

Recent research on transportation has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability in network traffic. This study focuses on estimating the probability distribution of traffic volume at specific times and locations within a transportation network. A stochastic model is developed to capture the complex dynamics of traffic flow and reliability is assessed using a key performance metric. A practical approach is implemented to apply the stochastic model to real-world traffic scenarios through simulation. This method is further enhanced by an optimization technique to identify critical parameters that influence the probability distribution of traffic volume. A real-world case study is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accounting for uncertainty and reliability in network traffic analysis.

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree search time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence, the study finds that the algorithms' common thread is the generation of uniform spanning trees. This realization enables a reduction in computational effort by showing that the trees produced by these algorithms are statistically equivalent to those generated by the uniform spanning tree algorithm. This research further explores extensions to generate free uniform spanning trees, exhibiting statistical relationships among multiple methods.

This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal data points. We propose a novel approach, the MusicTM-Dataset pre-training scheme, to obtain high-quality cross-modal features by employing pre-training a encoder with a pre-existing large music dataset and then fine-tuning it on the MusicTM-Dataset. To validate our music dataset's value, our pre-training method is combined with existing music encoders and compared with the traditional music encoding methods. The experimental results demonstrate the significant enhancement brought by the MusicTM-Dataset.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration.

We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable refractive index and a defocusing cubic nonlinearity, dark solitons can exist and be stable in certain conditions. This contrasts with the situation where the nonlinearity is constant, as defined by the Nagy-Kibelnik equation, in which only one type of dark soliton can exist. The Nagy-Kibelnik equation itself reduces to the well-known DKP equation when soliton interaction is ignored. The stability of these dark solitons depends on how the light's intensity varies and the soliton's initial phase. We've found that when variable refractive index is present, gap solitons can exist and be stable, whereas in the nonvariable refractive index case, only one type of gap soliton can exist. Similar to the dark solitons, the stability of these gap solitons depends on the light's intensity variation, the soliton's initial phase, and the type of gap soliton.

This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to a recent research in this field. To this end, we introduce a system that enables seamless coordination between users and machines through the performance of natural actions within interactive visualizations. We have devised a protocol that facilitates communication between integrated components and enable them to work in unison. Furthermore, we have crafted a representation that captures the essence of guidance provided by machines and effectively translate it into behavior applicable in real-time. To achieve this goal, we have created a representation that encapsulates various forms of guidance and translates them into actionable instructions. We have implemented and demonstrated the effectiveness of our idea through a demonstration paper that showcases its capabilities in practice.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ, real-time temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical fiber temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The data show that even with a lack of specific interactions, condensate formation can occur through general principles. The thermodynamic properties of droplets are influenced by the overall abundance of involved molecules, even if the system contains multiple different components. The results indicate that there is a universal mechanism for condensate formation and that spontaneous assembly can be a general phenomenon in biological systems.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom selections influences performance; and how different finite element grid parameters including grid size, problem size, and heart model geometry affect the balance between computational time and problem scale. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for specific problem variants and different computer configurations.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinkage following microstructure fabrication poses a significant issue for accurate numerical modeling and predicting actual device behavior. This study is the first to demonstrate a novel method for the numerical simulation of microstructures subjected to mechanical stress, thereby allowing for the design of acoustic metagratings at MHz frequencies. Our results indicate that significant structure shrinkage affects the bandgap characteristics of acoustic metagratings and that accurate modeling is only achieved when both thermal expansion and mechanical deformation are taken into account. The introduction of an average density in the polymer material, along with modified material properties, allows for precise prediction of the bandgap frequency and angle from simulated data. This innovative approach may expand the scope of metaacoustics and other advanced technologies such as metamaterials and nanophotonics.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we manage to enhance this rate to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Under the condition that the frequencies are sufficiently low, by incorporating the principles of the Littlewood-Paley theory, we find that the solutions have properties belonging to certain Besov spaces of negative order and establish the most favorable $L^2$ decay rate.

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to develop flexible and high-density networks. Mobile IAB, which facilitates the connection of UEs in motion, holds potential as a suitable solution. This work takes a different approach from existing literature by providing a comprehensive overview of deploying mobile IAB by covering: the IAB standardization in 5G New Radio (NR); a classification framework for both fixed and mobile IAB; an extensive analysis of mobile IAB performance through simulations; and the open challenges and future aspects of mobile IAB. The proposed taxonomy organizes existing IAB research by categorizing different perspectives, while categorizing mobile IAB by the type of mobility involved. In terms of performance assessment, the authors analyzed mobile IAB deployments in urban environments, specifically buses to enhance passenger connectivity, which resulted in significantly improved throughput and latency in both downlink and uplink compared to other network configurations.

In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their behavior when influenced by different sampling methods and metrics, providing insights into which settings significantly affect performance and interact with each other. The ranking of influential parameters suggests an optimal order of tuning, and our results also shed light on the overall stability of the algorithms.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in real-world settings. In this research, we investigate how established RL methods fare when confronted with challenges inherent in the nature of open-world problems. By designing an 8-puzzle domain with unpredictable changes, we create a testing ground to evaluate the robustness of RL strategies. Our findings reveal that prior methods are ineffective in adapting to unexpected modifications and often require modification to successfully navigate this domain. Consequently, we propose a new approach, Adaptive RL with Transfer Learning, which enables easy integration of new experiences and domain knowledge. This transfer learning framework is combined with an attention mechanism and a linear dynamical system model to facilitate efficient use of experience resources. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the novel approach to be highly effective in adapting to diverse problem variants and also outperforms compared baselines in unknown environments. Our code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/jmohanty/8-puzzle-RL.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly tied to the distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions and Gevrey spaces, as observed in previous works. Moreover, the occurrence of these smooth waves is possible even when the initial conditions are relatively smooth, which contrasts with results indicating that large irregularities can be a prerequisite for the formation of singularities in certain cases.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results demonstrate the ability to manipulate linear polarization states and could benefit research on spin-orbit interactions and angular momentum in exciton-polariton systems.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. The specific focus lies within a particular class of nonlocal problems formulated within a given domain in higher dimensions. The formulation is based on an equation where the fractional Laplacian of a variable $u$ is equal to the sum of a nonlinear term that involves the norm of the variable's gradient and an additional parameter with an applied force function. The conditions of existence and non-existence are explored with varying coefficients in a specific mathematical framework and solutions to related problems from earlier works are provided.

The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing. This endeavour revealed challenges pertaining to data availability, credibility, and governance in the public sphere within South Africa. This research aims to address these concerns by presenting the successful implementation of a public-facing data platform as a model solution to the existing data-related problems.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have focused on merging data from different modalities like clinical indicators and imaging. Our own study aims to contribute to this effort by exploring the value of integrating multimodal information for retinal disease diagnosis and risk assessment. Building on the principles of multi-task deep learning models, we have developed a method that allows for the learning and integration of multiple information sources. Our results show that this approach leads to enhanced performance when compared to existing techniques that solely rely on single modalities. Furthermore, we have applied our model to identify and quantify risk factors for specific retinal diseases, which when combined yield a higher accuracy than the individual risks assessed through our model for each disease. Our proposed method's code and pre-trained models are freely accessible on GitHub, along with other supporting materials on our website.

X-ray images contain subtle indicators that can distinguish the severity of COVID-19. Extracting meaningful features from these images can enhance the accuracy of severity prediction. X-ray images offer limited visual differences between severe and mild cases, making it crucial to employ advanced techniques to extract relevant features and improve the accuracy of severity prediction. X-ray images are composed of noise along with essential information, hindering pure network performance. We applied a noise removal filter to remove noise and used the FastRCNN together with Region Proposal Network to extract essential features from noise-free images. The proposed model utilized transfer learning based on pre-trained models and network fine-tuning. The evaluation of our model on a public dataset demonstrated a high Area under the ROC curve value of 0.95, along with a low binary cross-entropy loss of 0.13. This model's effectiveness was verified through comparison with existing methods. We also developed a depth-wise separable convolutional neural network to improve model accuracy using noise-free features. The novel model showed improved performance with a higher AUC of 0.96 and reduced binary cross-entropy loss of 0.12.

We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies around the boundary of $\Omega$ as the associated wavenumbers $k$ increase without bound. If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove the existence of transmission eigenfunctions that become localized around the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the geometric patterns of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, require extensive labeling, and cannot effectively identify intents. We address two key challenges associated with identifying intents: 1) distinguishing between intended and unrelated content, and 2) creating coherent graphs to represent conversation contexts. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach, Multi-context Guided Graph Attention, which combines graph attention with machine learning to uncover new intent categories. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to existing methods using human-labeled data and intend to evaluate its performance further using pre-trained language models.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct relationship with the 3D Wronskian form of the Cauchy matrix variables. The explicit forms of the Lax pair, bilinear form, and zero-curvature condition are then obtained using the classical definition of the Cauchy matrix. The explicit 1-form of the Lax pair is used to derive the Lax equation from the Lax pair's partial differential equations. The explicit expressions for the Gaudin matrix and the Lax equation itself are then explicitly calculated in a 3D Wronskian form. The zero-curvature condition is also expressed in a 3D Wronskian form. The explicit expressions for the Gaudin matrix and the Lax equation itself are then explicitly calculated in a 3D Wronskian form.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation extracted from a state $\rho_{AB}$ through a sequence of weak measurements, each characterized by an operator $\mathcal{E}\left(\rho_{AB}\right)$. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) in $\rho_{AB}$, with a specific multiplier. This relationship enables the calculation of the TQD for complex multi-partite states from the weak-value matrix of a target observable. Furthermore, a condition is established to determine if a state is entangled based on the QCC and TQD values of locally inaccessible information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our proposal with numerical simulations based on a bi-partite state consisting of two qubits.

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in visual settings requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within those objects. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, built on established graph-based methods, is made up of multiple layers and can capture the complexity of social interactions. It can also be fine-tuned to recognize attributes of individual characters. An extensive dataset of social interactions, called CARIK, is presented to train and test the network. On a key task, our approach outperforms a alternative technique that doesn't utilize a structured graph.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, hierarchical relationships due to their restricted receptive field. A fully connected graph like the entire human body or the entire brain is challenging to model with current GNNs, leading to a key constraint of GNNs in computer vision: the size of the graph. Our proposed dynamic graph message passing network (DGPN) overcomes these limitations by enabling long-range relationship modeling in computer vision tasks. DGPN is a two-stage learning framework that generates node features and receives messages from a global pool. It combines the benefits of CNNs and GNNs by using CNNs to boost node features and GNNs for long-range relationship modeling. Through comprehensive experiments on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, we demonstrate that DGPN outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hedge row recognition, vehicle re-identification, and person re-identification. Our code and data sources are available for public access at the GitHub repository.

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the actual LUT-based area in Full Custom Place and Route environments. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations and enables the exploration of near-optimal solutions for widely used constants.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research and identifies existing knowledge gaps. Furthermore, the paper speculates on future developments and potential applications of quantum deep learning technology.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics, serving not only existing but also future experiments.
Recent breakthroughs in RF technology have facilitated proposals and upgrades for 
future particle physics experiments, notably influencing the design of the Fermilab 
PIP-II project, the European XFEL, and future circular e+ collider (FCCee).
This presentation will overview the advancements in RF technology, specifically in 
switching, shared, and cavity design, and highlight the innovations introduced 
by the Fermilab PIP-II project and the European XFEL, particularly in switching 
systems and high-power shared networks, and their implications for future 
accelerator applications.

In the near future, physicists anticipate the discovery of new physics beyond the Standard Model at high-energy colliders such as the LHC and lepton colliders like CLIC and ILC. To efficiently extract the full potential of these experiments, it's crucial to develop optimized reconstruction techniques for measuring the properties of massless lepton pairs produced through various weak interactions. For this reason, researchers are developing a novel method using matrix calculations that can efficiently handle challenging processes even with low signal-to-noise ratios. This matrix approach has proven its effectiveness in several tests using actual detector simulations for three different detector setups, achieving superior results compared to current statistical methods. This study directly addresses noise and systematic uncertainties common in actual detector environments, providing valuable tools for both theoretical and experimental physicists.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Our research offers a novel explanation for the observed diffuse radio signal, which could be attributed to the Hawking radiation of primordial black holes. Assuming all dark matter exists as these black holes, we calculate that the temperature resulting from their evaporation would be sufficient to produce the required signal. This temperature is identical to the one previously estimated for explaining the observed diffuse gamma-ray background. Primordial black holes possess a distinct property - their ability to evaporate - which distinguishes them from other forms of matter. This process results in a predictable and well-understood phenomenon known as Hawking radiation. We demonstrate that the diffuse radio signal can be explained by this same process, which has previously been proposed as a potential source of the diffuse gamma-ray background. This hypothesis suggests that primordial black holes have a significant impact on fundamental physics due to their large estimated mass density. Previous research has estimated that these black holes comprise approximately 85% of dark matter in the universe. We begin by reviewing the properties of Hawking radiation, which suggests that these black holes would have evaporated completely in the past. This leads to a prediction that the universe should be filled with a diffuse gamma-ray background, which has been extensively studied and which our hypothesis cannot explain. We rule out a similar explanation for the diffuse high-energy neutrino background. We confirm that the diffuse high-energy gamma-ray background can be explained by the decay of topological defects, and we find that this explanation is consistent with recently released data. We also examine the

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. The VSP safeguardingly shields both input data and function evaluations against adversaries in a secure computing offloading scenario like cloud computing. To enhance performance, our innovative VSP architecture features a five-stage pipeline design that increases circuit evaluation parallelism. Moreover, a custom-designed Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) was created to decrease processor gate count, accompanied by comprehensive toolchains allowing for arbitrary C program compilation into our custom ISA. To further boost performance, CMUX Memory-based ROM and RAM implementations were developed, replacing traditional sequential ROM and RAM. Experimentation results confirm the effectiveness of the VSP in achieving substantial speedups compared to other FHE-based solutions.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for Baker's method and extended it to more general graph classes. We enhance the simpler approach to work without utilizing the connectivity restriction, resulting in a PTAS for any graph class. 

Our solution builds on previous work by Bulatov and Zhuk, who translated the PTAS for Maximum Independent Set to CSPs with specific constraints. We generalize their results to a broader class of constraints, allowing arbitrary properties of the independent set. Furthermore, we prove that Bulatov and Zhuk's theorem is strictly limited, as we show that certain'simple' constraints cannot be satisfied through PTAS reductions.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to address the limitation of UPOA and UPIO in handling short sentences. Extensive evaluations on various English datasets reveal that UPIO surpasses existing unsupervised and few-shot parsing models in terms of performance.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification.
