This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, which facilitates efficient object segmentation within complex urban environments. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding segmentation framework, we demonstrate how these images can improve low-quality labels, ultimately leading to higher accuracy in object segmentation. Our results illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in urban settings, which significantly surpasses the performance of standard RGB-image-based object segmentation methods. This phenomenon is attributed to the enhanced spectral resolution of HSI images, which facilitates better understanding and more accurate learning of complex urban street-parking scenarios. This research validates the significant potential of HSI images in computer vision applications, showcasing improved performance over standard RGB images in object segmentation tasks. The code and data used in this study have been made publicly available for reference at the specified links.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, found no significant variations in its chemical composition, and utilized 3D stellar modeling to simulate its surface and internal rotation rates. Our main findings are aligned with the observed rotational rate disparity, suggesting that differential rotation and tidal forces may be responsible for this unusual behavior. Moreover, our models predict that we should be able to detect spectral line broadening and variations in optical and ultraviolet light emission in the next few years, which will provide further clues to understanding the star's behavior.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. Our proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after initial linear-time processing. Additionally, despite the limited storage capacity, our RAM model can accommodate and process large amounts of data through a combination of division-based algorithms and dynamic register management.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item a user will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and computable in explicit terms. Our integrals have further significant mathematical implications, including reconnecting Borel's cohomology with Chow's and Kerz's work, linking Gromov-Witten invariants with cohomology via the Grothendieck-teichmüller group and Motivic Galois group, and generalizing it to the Deligne-Mumford stack of representations over the general linear group.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems and found that correlations can be described through a non-Hermitian symmetry, which we refer to as "PT symmetry" under distinct conditions. By applying this formulation, we derived an extended classification protocol for one-dimensional systems that considers both local constraints and symmetry requirements. Notably, our research reveals that correlations can alter a system's topological characteristics, resulting in a larger class of topological phenomena. We substantiate the theoretical framework by presenting a number of meaningful examples. The outcomes of our study demonstrate that dynamically generating correlations via unitary transformations can yield diverse topological properties. Consequently, we propose the idea that "topological flexibility" can be achieved through correlations, which may provide new perspectives for experimental design and topological system development.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $f(n)$ be the count of unique ways to express numbers in the set $\mathcal{S}$ as sums of squares with addends being non-negative integers. We represent each count as a function $g(n)$ and assert that $g(n)$ can be expressed through a convolution of two functions, one of which is equivalent to $g(\sqrt{n})$. It is demonstrated that the count $f(n)$ grows at a rate exceeding linear growth, thereby proving a long-standing conjecture proposed by Allen Schanzenbach. Moreover, we show that for a given positive integer $k$, the count $f_{k}(n)$, which corresponds to representations with addends being $k$-linear combinations of integers, also grows at a rate exceeding linear growth.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice relaxation and changes in the electron density in the core, along with optimized core-orbital replacements, were considered to determine ground state properties of paired phosphorus dopants in silicon through a unified approach.
The results show that binary pairs with n^0 and spin exchange coupling capabilities can form a bond at the distance of about 3.5 silicon lattice units, and those with n^+ and spin exchange coupling capabilities, an bond at the distance of about 3.6 silicon lattice units.
The calculated energies of the first excited states for both binary pairs matched the experimental results, and the obtained values were close to the results obtained from coupled-electron pair calculations, showing agreement within 5%.
The studies on triplets and quartets showed that Coulomb interactions, which can be adjusted through relaxation, determine the first excited states, however the inherent tunneling properties of silicon determines the ground states, proving that single-dopant-based approaches are insufficient to precisely determine the properties of paired dopants, and a paired-dopant-only framework is necessary for a comprehensive understanding.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors.  We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser.  Due to its two-photon nature, the technique confines
charge carrier generation in 3-D around the laser focal point.  This localized
charge injection enables us to study the semiconductor bulk with high 3-D
resolution.  We mapped the diamond's bulk electrical field at varying depths by
taking advantage of charge spatial confinement.  The results show that the
technique can be utilized to investigate charge transport in micro- and nano-
electronic devices with high spatial resolution, particularly deep junctions.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three different models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs, employing a BERT-based encoder and a linear classifier for the classification task. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieve top-tier outcomes, with an impressive macro F1 score of 78.58 in the test set, earning us second place in the competition.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and various combinatorial methods, offering flexibility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we propose a new caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and near constant transmission rates using a specific type of arithmetic sequence. Additionally, we modify this framework to be applicable to the distributed computation problem. A novel transmission method in the shuffle phase is presented, demonstrating the potential for reduced communication load compared to existing methods with similar file counts.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been extended to a specific set of representations, which can be thought of as a middle ground between non-degenerate and degenerate cases. This extension is made possible by a new approach that simplifies the complex calculation typically associated with this type of series. Our work also relies on a significant contribution from a mathematical concept called the local archimedean part of the adelic group, as set out by Darmon and Diamond.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital representations, despite the inherent intricacies and ambiguities. This work delves into using graph-based algorithms and graph neural networks as innovative solutions for resolving the challenges inherent in NLP, specifically graph neural networks. Our primary focus lies on applying graph neural networks to the essential task of text summarization via the selection of crucial sentences. To this end, we've developed three novel approaches. Firstly, we utilized sentence co-occurrence data to create a sentence similarity graph based on the two common metrics of Cosine Similarity and Jaccard Index. Secondly, we created a fine-grained graph by combining sentences using multi-graph techniques. Finally, we employed graph neural networks to determine sentence importance, followed by extensive evaluations on real-world datasets, yielding impressive results that surpass existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a significant contribution from very low $p_T$ photons.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the codegree vector's l1-norm in 3-uniform hypergraphs containing no K4^3. The resulting extremal function represents a trade-off between two extremal functions introduced by Allen and Beecher, and can be computed using a randomized algorithm that determines extremal hypergraphs with linear asymptotic extremality. We also demonstrate that similar approaches can be applied to calculate the extremal extremality of higher degree sums in n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraphs.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results. As a result, there is a pressing need to identify a suitable anti-aliasing method for vector maps. This study aims to address this need by evaluating four spatial anti-aliasing algorithms and integrating them into a proposed workflow. Furthermore, the research presents a technical solution to overcome the limitations posed by the lack of a, a failure to preserve original colors, and b constraints imposed by the OpenGL API. Specifically, the study introduces a new multi-pass rendering approach, an essential component of the proposed workflow. Additionally, the research tackles the challenges of determining the optimal number of samples and texture size for spatial anti-aliasing. Experimentally validated results confirm that the proposed workflow outperforms existing techniques in terms of visual quality and system efficiency.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we define a novel, transcendental interpolation function, derived from the hyperbolic tangent, that seeks to minimize relative differences. It's shown that this new function yields more efficient approximations than the classic multiquadric, in terms of accuracy and the number of evaluations needed. Furthermore, we prove that as the dimension increases, the hyperbolic tangent-based method converges at a faster rate than the multiquadric.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their long-term propagation. The identification of pulsar halos remains challenging due to their impermanence and the lack of comprehensive sky coverage above a certain energy threshold. We propose an advanced method to detect pulsar halos that incorporates Monte Carlo simulations, aligned with real X-ray data from Chandra and Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations. The star-forming region of the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex is studied as a case study to illustrate the effectiveness of this analytical method.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate concern, as seen in the decline from 2007 to 2012 in Europe and from 2012 to 2015 in the US. Conversely, scientists' climate interest has consistently increased over time. Furthermore, we find that scientists' and the general public's interests in climate change do intersect and influence each other.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. This study presents a novel control algorithm that relies on control barrier functions to enable soft grippers to successfully pick up a wide range of objects. The proposed approach considers the inherent uncertainties and constraints inherent in soft grippers and their actuators. Through simulation and real-world experiments, the effectiveness of this control method has been validated for both sphere-like and irregular objects.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple parameter spaces. Our work builds upon this idea by introducing a novel method using orthogonal basis functions to express the mapping between original and equivalent parameter spaces. Furthermore, we employ a Bayesian approach to estimate the mapping and the uncertainty associated with it, thus making progress in two related fields: Bayesian estimation and optimization simultaneously.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies can illuminate distant spaces. This study explores the possibility that a particular ancient galaxy, identified as a faint millimeter wave source (WISEJ171337.76+63061), is actually a very young and densely structured black hole complex, given its rapid light variations and distinct spectral patterns. This would make it one of the earliest stages of jet activity in the universe, providing a unique chance to study how galaxies and black holes develop.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we apply a series of data augmentation techniques to improve the model's ability to handle untested wavelengths and density configurations. This research showcases the feasibility of using machine learning to analyze observed quasar spectra and its potential to expand the spatial coverage of cosmological density perturbation analysis beyond what traditional methods can attain.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to the Lie algebra of 12x12 upper triangular matrices over a three-dimensional field with one parameter. Firstly, we identify all possible irreducible modules resulting from the product of two modules: one that is a highest weight module with quasi-finite properties and the other a module that is free in relation to U(H). Secondly, using braiding symmetry associated with the algebra, we establish which specific conditions must be met for the product of three modules to be individually irreducible. Additionally, a category consisting of U(H)-free modules with the properties of finite length and containing the module generated by a single element with no Annihilator, is introduced and we study the central lemmas within this category.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large pre-trained language models, thereby enabling open-domain dialogue models
to fulfill role requirements with minimal additional training samples. Our
experiments show that our approach allows the models to consistently demonstrate
assigned roles while maintaining natural human conversation on a large scale.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; however, it provides a different theory that predicts the universe's supersymmetry will decay in a phase transition. This supersymmetry decay could create gravitational waves that were produced during the universe's early stages, potentially detectable by future observations; moreover, these conditions could create an environment in which certain types of dark matter can form more easily, specifically the universe's primordial form of dark matter known as WIMPs.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game between a transmitter and receiver with limited knowledge of each other's intentions. Transmitters utilize simple, visually perceivable signals to convey information, and receivers learn to recognize essential parameters by interacting with the transmitters. Performance is measured by the receivers' ability to accurately interpret the transmitted information and the minimal amount of information exchanged to achieve this. Computational power is also taken into consideration when evaluating the receivers' performance. Simulation results demonstrate that this transparent and real-time semantic communication system produces high-quality information with minimal data transfer and information exchange, and performs better than conventional methods such as pure amplitude phase (AAP) and active and passive learning techniques.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here leverages the efficiency of syntactic tree-based methods and the power of semantic analysis, using just three fundamental matrix operations. Furthermore, this model's speed is comparable to that of leading machine learning-based solutions. Evaluations using three widely-used metrics reveal that our proposed model achieves performance on par with state-of-the-art solutions.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles: when the dimer is aligned, it moves along the gradient, but when it's offset, it moves in a circular motion. Some dimers exhibit a simple superposition of these behaviors, but others display more intricate dynamics. The outcome depends on the activity level and the presence of activity gradients, as well as the type of force affecting the dimer, whether attractive or repulsive. Some dimers may seek equilibrium by aligning in the gradient and assuming a fixed shape, while others may maintain an offset configuration and circle around while remaining a fixed distance apart. In cases where activity levels are moderate, we found that the dimensionless force from the gradient can be compared to an effective force that keeps dimers aligned, and this comparison can predict whether dimers circle or move straight. The potential for mapping this prediction to different physical scenarios is also explored.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 257 fractures.

Advanced autonomic swarms comprised of autonomous drones exhibit sophisticated behavior when executing complex operations such as structural coverage in search and rescue missions.  To ensure seamless collaboration among these drones, researchers have introduced various social behavior models.  Existing literature focuses primarily on collision avoidance through inter-drone communication, neglecting the benefits of tapping into their collective knowledge.  This paper introduces a wavefront search algorithm enabling optimized path planning during navigation, and integrates it into a collective awareness framework.  Our proposed approach incorporates a shared map of the environment, and utilizes the shared knowledge of the swarm's position and number of members.  Simulation results demonstrate that our wavefront-based algorithm is equal to or more effective than other path planning methods in collective awareness scenarios.  Furthermore, our model outperforms existing social behavior models utilizing shared knowledge, and offers a valuable resource for researchers in this field.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures. Our objective is to determine the optimal control that maximizes a cost function, subject to constraints imposed by the fractional Black-Scholes equation with a delay. This is made possible through the introduction of a Lagrangian and the use of a numerical method for differentiating functions of measures, allowing us to establish the existence of a unique Lagrange multiplier. To prove the reachability of the maximum, we employ a variational principle and establish the convergence of a specific algorithm, which involves the use of fractional Itō stochastic calculus, to obtain the optimal control. This algorithmic approach is further supplemented by the introduction of a numerical scheme based on the Lévy-Caratheodory type, which effectively circumvents the problem of computing the differential of a function of a measure.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak links to RSUs, and increased packet loss. Mobile vehicle relays can alleviate this issue by enhancing network performance for users in congested regions. While selecting relay nodes for data transfer is typically based on the quality of the link between the source and the relay, and between the relay and the RSU, the current research lacks a comprehensive study of relay node selection that considers data transfer between vehicles. In this paper, we propose an adaptive algorithm that uses a deep neural network to identify the optimal relay node for each user in congested areas. The proposed algorithm learns the characteristics of the network from ground truth data and estimates the link quality between vehicles and RSUs/relays in real-time. The results of the simulations indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, specifically in areas with high packet error rates and limited bandwidth. The success of the algorithm is measured by its ability to enhance the overall link quality, increase the successful data transfer rate, and reduce the latency in data transfer.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and the post-edit version as high quality. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields 0.042 accuracy in terms of edits, and 0.021 accuracy in terms of characters, although human annotations have significantly higher accuracy. Nonetheless, this is the first time that Wikipedia article enhancements have been automatically labeled on a large scale, totaling 248 million sentences. Furthermore, our data indicates that enhancements are predominantly additions of new information rather than deletions, and that article improvements are more likely to occur on low-quality articles.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for the model training. Experimental results show that the method achieves comparable results to traditional knowledge distillation methods while offering flexibility and potential applications in real-world and autonomous driving scenarios.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder performance. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that with optimal threshold spacing, search-limited sequential decoding achieves nearly identical error-correction performance as PACT Decentralized Maximum-Likelihood Decoding.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses simulated, highly variable synthetic data for ease of generalization, making our system more versatile. Our method performs well on real in-the-wild hand-object interaction datasets such as HO3D and DexYCB without further adjustments and significantly surpasses state-of-the-art depth-based hand and object tracking methods while operating at a high 9 FPS rate.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, 3, and 3 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. We investigate the resulting group, which we term G_{45,3,3,3}, with focus on its composition and properties. A previous study had proposed that G_{45,3,3,3} is isomorphic to the 29-reflective modular Weyl group of type G_{2,3}. Our research confirms this isomorphism and further reveals that G_{45,3,3,3} can be represented by the group of 29-reflective automorphisms of a specific diamond graph.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single cycle. A 3D detector is also developed to accurately track the end-effector's movement and temporarily store pose information until a rotation is detected, at which point the stored data is used for calibration. Our system's designs to handle end-effector look-at rotations through the incorporation of a rotation prediction module. It also features a choice of two advanced algorithms for end-effector position and rotation prediction that utilize keypoint detection and a pair of calibration algorithms to resolve ambiguity, including a method that utilizes a temporary storage to handle cases where predictions are inaccurate. Our system's designs to handle fiducial-free extrinsic calibration in a real-world setting, in a way that's distinct from simulation-based approaches. Through evaluation, it's shown that our system is capable of achieving high accuracy in a variety of scenarios and outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of both precision and processing speed.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees, 125 million galaxies, and 125 billion pixels. A four-step process, including source classification and shearing, photometry calculation, galaxy and lensing density map construction, and final weak-lensing map creation, has been applied to the UNIONS/CFIS data. Through this research, we identify a noticeable shear bias of $0.0065 \pm 0.0043$ and residual multiplicative shear bias of $0.0055 \pm 0.0043$ in the final weak-lensing maps. A comparison of our results with COSMOS shows comparable characteristics. To ensure accuracy, we employ a testing strategy, applying mock galaxies to the data and conducting extensive quality controls. The finished weak-lensing maps are based on a delensed sky, providing valuable resources for research and further study.

We examine the local behavior of the parity of the cardinalities of sets generated by the Rauzy vocabulary, in relation to irrational rotations of $[0,1)$ and $[0,\lambda)$. Let $\lambda$ be an irrational number, and $q$ be an natural number. The rotation maps $\rho_i^{\tau}$ for $0\leq i\leq 3$ are defined as follows: $\rho_0^{\tau}(x)=x+\tau$ and $\rho_i^{\tau}(x)=x+\tau+i\lambda$ for $i=1,2,3$. A sequence of words $w_0\cdots w_{p-1}$ in the Rauzy vocabulary is used to define the set $R(\tau,\lambda,p)$ as the intersection of the sets $x+\tau$ and the rotations of $x$ by multiples of $\lambda$. A number is chosen randomly from the set $\{0,\ldots,\lambda-1\}$, and for any given $k$, we let $N(r,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},k)$ be the count of numbers $p$ in the set $\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$ such that the parity of the cardinalities of $R(\tau,\lambda,p)$ and $\mathcal{A}(\tau,\lambda,p)$ and $\mathcal{B}(\tau,\lambda

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, a spin-lattice relaxation study, muon spin relaxation, and ac susceptibility all serve as key experimental techniques to determine the parameters of the BKT theory. Lastly, the temperature-dependent susceptibility shows a logarithmic increase in spin-correlation length below the critical temperature, consistent with a power-law behavior expected in 2D physics.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. We present a detailed analysis of natural, fine-tuned, and weakly-interacting massive particles within the $a$MSM model, and our findings reveal that natural dark matter is achievable at a much lower scale than previously thought, specifically below 10^9 GeV. Furthermore, even in the fine-tuned scenario, a massive stabilizer axion can be produced with a pivot point at 10^9 GeV, and simultaneously explaining both dark matter and axion-related phenomena is possible through a heavy neutrino with a mass of approximately 5*10^14 GeV.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. By integrating this enhanced bound into the previously described simulation algorithms, we achieve a significant decrease in the resource requirements for simulating circuits comprising up to $n$ qubits and $k$ levels of T gates. The modified algorithms can execute in time $O(2^{0.198n})$ and $O(2^{0.288k})$, respectively.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, namely non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the quintessence field effect: the complex and real parts. We assume the real part 
behaves as a slow-roll field.
We understand that scenarios with a fractional energy density ($\Omega_{D} > 1$) do not 
accurately depict real universes. Furthermore, we introduce an interacting coupling 
parameter, $b^{2}$, linked to the Tsallis model's constant parameter ($\delta$) with 
respect to a fractional energy density ($0.73$).
Notably, unlike real quintessence, we identify an interdependence between the fractional 
energy density, interacting coupling, and other parameters in this theory.
Ultimately, we visually illustrate and compare ($\omega-\omega'$) and ($\nu_{s}^{2}$) 
characteristics in two scenarios, highlighting their distinctions.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware random number generators. Nevertheless, the reliance of these TRNGs on consumer products raises significant privacy concerns, given their potential for being manipulated by untrustworthy entities. This paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG designed to mitigate prior vulnerabilities, which generates a bit based on a poor man's random principle to access an SRAM cell. To start, the TRNG produces a random bit that determines whether to use a fast but unreliable or a slower but more reliable access method to the SRAM. This initial random bit also decides whether to process the SRAM access as a rising or falling edge of a clock signal. While previous SRAM-based TRNGs have relied on fluctuating supply voltages or temperature readings, which can be tampered with, this new approach uses solely clock manipulation to ensure the SRAM access is unpredictable. This TRNG can operate at either high-speed or high-reliability settings, depending on whether the initial random bit generates a 0 or 1, respectively. Furthermore, the TRNG produces an entropy-rich bit that is converted into a random number, which is then post-processed using a limited-memory FPGAs-based health check to guarantee its unpredictability, even in case of potential side-channel attacks.
