The distinctive properties of massive atmospheres offer a novel tool for assessing the presence of thick H2 envelopes in sub-Neptune exoplanets through observations of their atmospheres, particularly regarding the atmospheric composition and temperature profile.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The synapse with the most significant difference in firing rates between the two neurons it connects, in comparison to the average synapse, is selected for weight adjustments during the learning process. As a result of this focused update mechanism, the synapses with the greatest asymmetry in connection strengths exhibit the most rapid improvements during the learning process. Our study has demonstrated that this MPN is capable of learning various temporal patterns in line with their original temporal structure, and its efficacy has been verified through both numerical simulations and formal analytical proofs. Furthermore, numerical investigations have revealed that the MPN is able to identify key temporal features even in the presence of significant noise, as well as observe recurring patterns in periodic stimuli and differentiate between distinct sequences.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating and efficiently computing separate paths for multiple dynamical systems with uncertain parameters. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research returns to a renowned model for tumor-induced death in unicellular organisms and uses two distinct approaches for computing chaos expansions. Additionally, this study presents results on the $S$-shape profile characteristic of this model, which indicates that the shape's appearance is highly sensitive to parameter values.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an adaptive monitoring system capable of handling high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. Our proposed solution incorporates the Shiryaev-Roberts method at the failure mode level and employs multi-arm bandit strategies to balance discovery and exploitation. Furthermore, our algorithm's theoretical underpinnings demonstrate its efficacy in isolating the primary failure mode. Through simulations and case studies, we verify that the detection performance of changes and accuracy in isolating the failure mode can be substantially enhanced.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that are now integrated into the Milky Way's outer regions: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on accurate measurements of their surviving star clusters and mixed stellar content. By mimicking the process of material accumulation at the galaxies' outer edges, we've determined the timescales for their infall: 10 billion years for Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and 7-9 billion years for Wukong/LMS-1. These models also allow us to explore the possibility of a gravitational interaction between the two galaxies, which we've determined would not significantly affect the other. Our findings, however, do indicate that both galaxies initially followed an unusual development pattern, characterized by rapid growth in certain areas, which we're investigating further to better understand their distinct shapes and movements.

Given a profinite group G, we've established an extension of the homotopy orbit spectral sequence, applicable when H satisfies a specific finiteness condition for an S[[G]]-module H. This generalizes the homotopy orbit spectral sequence in the case of a finite group G. The extension is expressed through the realization of a certain differential graded profinite G-spectrum, which we term {\mathfrak{R}}(H). The properties of {\mathfrak{R}}(H) are investigated, including its realization as a suspension of a profinite G-spectrum derived from the Bousfield localization of H, and its expression as an extension of the Borel equivariantized suspension spectrum of H. The properties of the homotopy orbit spectral sequence are also explored, such as its degeneration under specific conditions and its degeneration when G is finite, as well as its degeneration when H meets certain finiteness conditions as a G-spectrum. The applications of the theorem to the case of a finite group G are also outlined, resulting in the recovery of several significant theorems, including the Sullivan-Taylor theorem and the Borel Hurewicz theorem.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the number of documents that need to be annotated. This method identifies the most relevant documents based on the accuracy of their already labeled information and selectively allows those that are likely to contain errors in order to label them. Our experiments on a real-world invoice dataset demonstrate that Selective Labeling can enhance data accuracy while minimizing costs compared to traditional full-labelling methods.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnitude of the magnetic moment is relatively low.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are becoming increasingly popular due to their exceptional performance in various applications. However, they are notoriously difficult to train, requiring an inordinate amount of computational resources and extensive time. Current training frameworks often struggle to handle inference tasks, particularly when dealing with large datasets and processing demands. To address these challenges, we present ClickTrain, a proprietary training system, and a complementary inference framework, SemAnt, both developed by Google researchers. By integrating these tools, we achieve substantial speedups in training and inference times, outperforming existing frameworks and models. The SeAnt framework is particularly effective in large-scale systems, with which we have broken numerous ImageNet Challange record benchmarks.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel deep learning methods based on recurrent neural networks that can accurately detect signals from real datasets from the Gravitational Wave Open Data project with high confidence levels. Our approach outperforms conventional methods by a substantial margin and provides statistically significant results.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by remaining in its original location rather than being formed by a specific high-energy migration mechanism. Further study found that the host star, which is approximately 10 billion years old, has a metal composition that deviates from a commonly recognized trend of metal-rich giant planets being formed around metal-rich host stars. Interestingly, this study found that both heavy and lightweight gas giants orbiting either warm or hot stars have higher-than-average metal compositions. TOI-5542b is a notable addition to studies of planetary composition due to its relatively cool temperature, which prevents it from expanding in size as a result of exposure to its star's heat.

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs: determining the optimal policy and uncertainty regarding state observations. To tackle these challenges, we develop a new algorithm based on the factoring of CMDPs. This approach breaks down the CMDP into two separate components: a stochastic dynamic game and a structured conditional probability model. We then use a general factorization condition to establish the optimal policy and state observation variables for any given game. This factorization enables us to design a new algorithm that determines the optimal policy while addressing observation uncertainty. Ultimately, this approach reduces the complexity of solving factorable CMDPs by transforming the original problem into a sequence of simpler game problems.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many mathematical symbols require connection and are part-based, we focus on recognizing single characters and groups of characters. We developed and tested this method on 518 equations from 116 mathematics textbooks, gathered from datasets and online resources. To evaluate our method, we applied traditional metrics used in handwriting recognition, such as deletion, insertion, and substitution rates, and also introduced a new error metric that takes into account the specific challenges of mathematical symbols. Our experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves high precision and efficiency in recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, even with simple smartphone camera technology. The total processing time is under 1 second, making it suitable for use in smartphone apps.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics.

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation 
in a model where contact rates are randomly generated and tied to network topology. 
Our study reveals that dissimilar network designs significantly influence the prevalence 
of outbreaks, often yielding lower epidemic rates than uniform networks. Moreover, 
we observe that in networks where connection probability decreases with distance from the center, 
pandemics may come close to reaching complete coverage without necessarily spreading 
through the entire network. Our findings also indicate that the spread of information 
or diseases can be accelerated by adjusting the underlying network layout.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often lacks sufficient efficiency. Integrating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) actor-critic (AC) provides significant advantages over traditional actor-critic methods. By merging the two concepts, a new, more effective search strategy is achieved, allowing for greater exploration in the policy space. Consequently, this integrated approach, referred to as HMC-AC, enhances sample efficiency and reduces variable bias. Furthermore, a bridge-based operator is developed to facilitate exploration of the continuous action space. Experimental evaluations using standard benchmark tests indicate substantial improvements in both convergence speed and accuracy when compared to standard actor-critic methods.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of $k$ rather than $p$ can make identifying them more efficient. This paper seeks to explore and establish methods for obtaining large numbers of twin primes at specific levels of $k$.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, at the wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by accounting for both crystalline and amorphous water ice, as well as taking into account the influence of sub-micron grain sizes. Furthermore, combining magnetite with components of the CM2 chondrite Murchison offers a feasible framework for understanding the spectral variations among objects like Nereid, particularly in those with neutral-sloped spectra. It's worth noting that magnetite provides a fitting explanation of Nereid's spectral continuum, eliminating the necessity of incorporating Tholin-like organic substances. Our analysis also reveals that non-ice components of outer solar system bodies may closely resemble those found in carbonaceous chondrites, as proposed by Fraser et al. (

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find $(q+1)^{(n-1)}q^{\frac{3(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}$ affine planes of order $q$, where points and lines within such a plane satisfy specific submodule properties. These affine planes are ultimately shown to be extendable to a projective plane of order $q$, where points and lines within such a plane satisfy specific submodule properties.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within these models.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key quantity known as the Q-function, accurately estimating the Q-function is often challenging. Our approach uses a new variational expectation maximization algorithm that circumvents the need to estimate the Q-function. By incorporating offline data and a new pessimism-based loss function, our approach optimizes the dynamic treatment regimes with reduced risk. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in various data sets, and we further analyze its performance with a comprehensive set of empirical studies.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through the application of the bosonization method, we obtained an analytical understanding of the system's properties, including the emergence of Dirac II superconducting phases with monopole vortices and pseudo-dilution magnetic effects. Furthermore, our results show that the system transitions into topological superconducting phases upon doping, characterized by the presence of Majorana edge modes responsive to electromagnetic fields.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, linguistic analyses, and social science investigations. Clustering methods can effectively categorize similar patterns or items within a set, and this work focuses on evaluating the effectiveness of eight popular clustering approaches using different metrics on real-world and generated presence-absence data. The goals of this research include (1) identifying suitable presence-absence data analysis methods, (2) investigating the sensitivity of clustering outcomes to varying data resampling techniques, and (3) determining whether external validation of clusters aligns with internally derived results.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics.

The UM-IU NLP group's competitive machine learning models for SemEval 2019 join the conversation: stance detection in social media join the conversation, which included subtasks that required detecting stance towards immigration and climate change in tweets. We employed fine-tunedbert-base-robusta and crf-classifiers to detect abusive content, along with a combination of pre-trained and custom features to address subtasks. Our primary tool was custom Python environment for NLP, and we conducted experiments using a dataset from Twitter's Hortonworks. We achieved notable results in subtasks, but did not achieve top rankings in the competition. This paper outlines our approach, presents the results, and offers future directions.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N. We achieve analogous results when examining quotients of numbers whose binary format is anti-palindromic, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In addition, several numerical data points, as well as intriguing hypotheses and areas for further investigation, are provided.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and materials. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates across different subjects and materials, the process of reconstructing images becomes inherently complex. Owing to the widespread availability and high flux of such X-ray sources, partially polyenergetic, fan-beam scanners have become particularly common in various applications. Nevertheless, the partially polyenergetic nature of these scanners gives rise to additional artifacts during image reconstruction, which can be rectified through the implementation of accurate mathematical formulations. However, these formulations often necessitate an a priori knowledge of transmission maps, which can be both challenging and time-consuming to obtain. In our research, we introduce a novel, iterative algorithm that accounts for both the energy-dependent attenuation and the scattering effects present during X-ray propagation. Replacing traditional binning techniques with our method allows for accurate attenuation maps to be derived from limited measurements, effective in addressing artifacts stemming from incomplete measurement data. The proposed algorithm's performance has been thoroughly evaluated against established benchmark procedures for both noise-free and noise-contaminated conditions.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with more precise limits in ab initio calculations. Our scheme enables us to reach higher energies of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements, $E_{\max$3}$, than was previously possible. We have demonstrated that our storage approach leads to converged calculations for the binding energy of the $^{3}$He ground state. Our results show that we can accurately calculate three-nucleon interactions up to an energy of $E_{\max$3}$ = 75 MeV, matching experimental measurements. Our study also explores the connection between the convergence of the path-integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) and configuration-interpolation (CI) methods, based on the maximum three-nucleon interaction energy, $E_{\max$3}$. Our findings indicate that the PIMC/CI convergence accelerates as $E_{\max$3}$ increases, suggesting a future merger of the two methods at higher $E_{\max$3}$ levels.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to the four-point function, specifically a specific combination of 'non-symmetric' coefficients. Consequently, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to the four-point function, specifically a specific combination of 'non-symmetric' coefficients.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given size.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a linear combination of U(1)y and U(1)lepton, and derive the resultant quantum numbers for various fermions and gauge bosons. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a new heavy scale M-X. Our study focuses on two specific models: U(1)X+S+M-X and U(1)X+N+M-X, which can be examined through high-energy colliders such as LHC, a 100 TeV future hadron collider, and even through observations of stars and galaxies. Furthermore, even at M-X >> m_H, we find that the Higgs boson still receives a finite radius from the effects of M-X. Our investigation also reveals that the U(1)X current can be probed by searching for deviations in the Z boson decay width when m_X < 10 TeV. Lastly, we examine the possibility of remaining new physics above 10 TeV or even at M-X.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to data size, and this bound precisely estimates the original MARmax value. Additionally, our solution facilitates the rapid computation of features' marginal influences, which are essential for the analysis of MARmax and its reduction in specific scenarios. Experimental validation shows that our method efficiently calculates MARmax on diverse datasets and suggests useful features for reducing the bound on MARmax, thereby guiding future data collection.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered.

In a specific context related to generalized quadrangles, researchers seek codes with a minimum distance of 4 or greater, and based on the available data, it appears that the maximum length of such codes is equal to the minimum distance. We have found that the maximum length of codes with a distance of 4 is equal to the minimum distance, and we can explain this by demonstrating a maximum code with specific properties. Additionally, it is known that codes with a distance of 5 can have a length up to 5, and we have developed a method to identify all possible code maximums of distance 5. Understanding the nature of these code maximums enables us to make statements regarding the existence of ovoids and spread pairs in the quadrangle $W_4(3)$. Furthermore, it is known that codes with a distance of 6 can have a length up to 6, and it is proposed that code maximums of distance 6 are equivalent to the maximum number of 6-chains in the quadrangle $W_4(3)$, and based on this, we can determine the number of code maximums of distance 6. It is also known that codes with a distance of 7 can have a length up to 7, and it is proposed that code maximums of distance 7 are equivalent to the maximum number of 7-chains in the quadrangle $W_4(3)$, and based on this, we can determine the number of

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm 1/h}$ at which the correlation function transitions from a positive to a negative trend, it was determined that gas in the CMZ is organized in elongated structures. This angle, not far from the predicted value based on N-body simulations of the CMZ, including hydrodynamic effects, suggests that gas in the CMZ is largely driven by gravitational anisotropy. It was also observed that the density structure of gas in the CMZ is characterized by a scale similar to that of ionized gas and a smaller scale compared to radio continuum emission. This compares favourably with the scale of gas motion as reported by star-forming activity in the CMZ. By examining the spatial distribution of gas in the CMZ, it was noted that gas is missing from the north-east section of the CMZ, where it was speculated that this could be attributed to the influence of a galactic bar.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on a molecular or atomic level in this scenario, but the interplay between electronic relaxation and nuclear motion poses significant challenges to theoretical models. Our study explores the interplay between electronic dynamics and nuclear motion in nitrogen gas using a table-top X-ray source, creating an adjustable environment that mirrors the conditions found in certain free-electron laser experiments. Our findings demonstrate that the motion of nuclei within a N$_2$ molecule is not solely responsible for changes observed in the absorbed X-ray spectrum as a result of increasing flux, but rather that electronic relaxation dynamics, namely the re-establishment of the electronic band gap, contributes significantly to these changes. Our work showcases a unique approach to studying fast electronic dynamics using XANES, an effect that is distinct from transmission experiments, and further validates the assumptions underlying the development of optical saturable absorption layers using nitrogen gas.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, its ability to monitor both N-type and P-type device thermal activity enables isolation of temperature-related voltage and frequency variations. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, 100ns conversion time, 65.5nW power consumption, and an integrated 6-bit digital backend. Furthermore, the design's subtractive architecture and digital backend facilitate direct calculation of temperature-related voltage and frequency biases.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are comprised of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing different optical scissors types, and discuss the benefits and constraints of these implementations, with a focus on improving stability and heralding capabilities.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm in one dimension, showing that there's a threshold of n = 2^ℓ for ε = 2^(-ℓ) below which certain algorithms become significantly more efficient. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors prove that the competitive ratio of any online Euclidean (1+ε)-spanner algorithm is at least Ω(ε^(-1) (log n / log ε^(-1)) in R^d for d ≥ 2, provided that n is large enough. Sleator and Tarjan's O(log n / log (1+ε)) competitive ratio upper bound applies generally, the authors observe, but it relies on specific properties not available in multi-dimensional spaces.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this study proposes adopting multiple loss measures according to device misidentification rates, thus introducing the concept of risk in IoT device classification. This is formulated as a combinatorial optimization issue and resolved using the CE stochastic optimization strategy, a novel, time-efficient algorithm. Using real-world traffic, the efficacy of the approach in choosing the optimal features to minimize misidentification risks within specific feature extraction cost limits is illustrated.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a particular type of posets. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, along with their respective classes of forest models. These studies generalize conventional relational semantics used in intutionistic modal and epistemic logics. The research specifically identifies maximal subvarieties of finite Godel algebras and their dual forest models. It is demonstrated that each of these subvarieties has a prelinear distributive lattice component with a standard relational semantics. The study further identifies some non-intutionistic properties of Godel modal logics, such as the possibility of distributing but not preserving the $\Box$ operator over the lattice operations.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. With a specified mean PBH mass, our analysis suggests that primordial black holes could produce about 4 times more microlensing events than stellar black holes. Our predictions are based on several possible values for the PBH-to-dark matter ratio and the mass distribution of these black holes. By running PopSyCLE with these variables, we found that the galactic lensing rate could be attributed to approximately 39% stellar black holes, 29% other types of compact objects, and 32% primordial black holes. Annual microlensing rates calculated by PopSyCLE for the Milky Way are as follows: 6.83 events per year for stellar black holes, 4.29 events per year for other types of compact objects, and 5.15 events per year for primordial black holes. These numbers are based on

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, in six different ranges of $d$, for various isotropic liquid crystalline phases and hexagonal and tetragonal packings of molecules. For all $d$ values, below a $50 \%$ packing density, we observed liquid crystalline hexagonal and tetragonal structures, nano-segmented domains, and a gas-like state at very low densities, whereas at higher densities, the system exhibited all three aforementioned liquid crystalline phases as well as a liquid without any internal structure. For $d$ equal to $0.9$, we observed three liquid crystalline hexagonal, tetragonal, and polar phases, characteristic of molecules with the largest and smallest spheres that are highly disparate in size. Additionally, below a $50 \%$ packing density, the system also displayed polar liquid crystalline structures. We discovered that the parameters of our model can be mapped onto the parameters of hard wedge-shaped molecules, found that the system's behavior is similar to that of hard conical molecules for smaller $d$ values, and that at higher packing densities, the system exhibits layers of

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions on the sphere relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions, expressed in terms of Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all three essential ingredients while accommodating two alternative light detection mechanisms. Additionally, our method enables the selection of detection mechanism on a case-by-case basis. Consequently, this approach opens up new avenues for low-light and non-destructive imaging of delicate samples.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. The stress generated during flow followed a predictable pattern, depending on the surface roughness and speed. Two distinct friction mechanisms were observed, one related to the deformation of bubbles at low speed and another at high speed, where the fluid started to slip over obstacles. The transition between these mechanisms, resulting in a change from linear to nonlinear stress behavior, occurred when the speed matched the order of magnitude of the gap size between obstacles. Furthermore, at high speeds, the stress developed during flow was independent of the gap size and was solely determined by the friction of the liquid on the obstacle. The stress values in this regime were comparable to those of other complex liquids with orders of magnitude higher. The observation of a stress value of 10^4 Pa and the associated flow behavior suggests that the fluid in this regime has a characteristics flow behavior similar to molecular glasses, while the stress values in other regimes were influenced by different physical phenomena such as Cassie's law and wet obstacle surface stress.

This report details our methods that led to 2nd and 3rd place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a simple yet efficient model for multi-task classification. This report outlines our strategy for handling the diverse nature of the dataset and presents details about our data processing methods, features extraction techniques, and how we leveraged metadata to enhance classification accuracy. Furthermore, we analyzed the effectiveness of different features in supporting our diagnosis decisions.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains with alternating masses. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce monotonic asymptotics, consistent with existing results. However, this cancellation may lead to charge density waves with large amplitude and slow approach to equilibrium, accompanied by the emergence of nanoptera when mass ratios satisfy a specific condition.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within the inflationary potential. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G to K_G is achieved by dividing both graphs into their respective pairings. A Hamiltonian path in K_G is termed the pair-Hamiltonian path or PH-path. A graph is said to possess the PH-property if it has a pair-Hamiltonian path. The goal is to identify the minimum degree of a graph G to ensure it has the PH-property. By examining the properties of a specific triangle-based structure, we determine that G must have a minimum degree of at least 3 together with the restriction that the trio's edge connection structure follows a specific pattern. Furthermore, we present the theoretical minimum degree as 3 plus a specific triplet arrangement constraint, thereby providing an essential criterion for the PH-property.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The model incorporates a two-way mixing angle that determines whether the wavepacket spreads or remains localized. The presence of an asymmetry-induced gap in the Hamiltonian leads to a fluctuation-free coherent spreading phase, during which the wavepacket remains concentrated in the middle site. When the wavepacket is initiated sufficiently close to the detrapping point, spreading is significantly impeded. To illustrate the impact of asymmetry, we compare this behavior with a purely coherent scenario in an effective one-dimensional Hamiltonian.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we introduce the DINO self-supervised method, a form of contrastive learning that doesn't necessitate hand-engineered proxies. DINO has produced remarkable results, with the ViT-Base model yielding an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluated as a k-NN classifier. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that the self-supervised ViT features obtained with DINO retain their effectiveness even when fine-tuned on downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection, outperforming convnets and other self-supervised methods.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the concept of semantic guidance (SEGA), allowing artists to blend multiple, varied image prompts and dictate how they should contribute to the generation process, thereby gaining greater control over image editing and generation. By combining multiple prompts, SEGA enables the generation of images not physically present in the training data and produces more accurate images by weighting individual prompts differently. To implement SEGA, we develop a novel diffusion model utilizing a weighted combination of multiple prompts, resulting in a complex high-dimensional space that guides image generation. SEGA's effectiveness is demonstrated through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, including the production of images not physically present in the training data and the generation of more accurate images through the weighting of different image prompts.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in our approach to uncertainty modeling. Building on the success of the year-to-date advances in Bayesian deep learning, we highlight key research findings and provide accessible training guides for practitioners. Furthermore, we outline promising roads for future research in the field.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter called "higgsian dark matter." We found that J/ψ into invisible particles can indicate the existence of a new neutrino state if certain specific conditions are met. Moreover, this decay can also provide evidence for the interaction of a new neutrino state with a specific type of gauge boson. Concerning dark matter, we observed that J/ψ into invisible particles essentially tests a specific set of interactions involving a particular type of vector boson and sub-GeV dark matter particles. We derived limits on the production cross-section of dark matter by J/ψ, which is in line with existing constraints from other experiments. Our research demonstrates the value of utilizing rare decays of heavy particles to gain insight into both dark matter and new neutrino states.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. The resulting images were analyzed to identify magnetic bright points, and their movements were tracked, capturing statistical data on their size, speed, and distribution patterns. The findings indicate that these particles exhibit normal or log-normal distributions in terms of their area and diameter, and their speed is influenced by the solar cycle, with faster and larger structures generally observed during solar maximum and dominated by smaller and slower entities during solar minimum. The results were compared with theoretical predictions and existing literature, and further discussed in the context of the models governing magnetic bright points' behavior.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless becomes quantum mechanically unstable under an external magnetic field, potentially releasing energy on a galactic scale. If the dark monopole's mass is within a specific range, it may lead to a significant reduction in the kinetic mixing value required to satisfy halo ellipticity constraints, subsequently resulting in the monopole's charge becoming proportional to its mass. This condition may result in the monopole's decay into dark particles, potentially violating constraints from direct dark matter detection experiments.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research has enormous potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. However, the diverse spatio-temporal data patterns present in the field pose significant challenges to the development of reliable models. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the use of video transformer architecture (Video Swin-Transformer), which enables direct processing of spatio-temporal data and yields enhanced accuracy in weather forecasting. By combining this approach with 2D vision transformer for spatial analysis and incorporating a temporal attention mechanism, we have achieved superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods in weather prediction tasks. Notably, our model has demonstrated remarkable success in predicting severe weather conditions such as cyclones and anticyclones, and accurately detects geographical features (like mountains) that may influence weather patterns. Furthermore, the spatial and temporal recurrence patterns in weather images can be effectively captured through the use of geometric transformers, and by integrating storm centers as additional input, we have significantly improved our results in predicting storm-related metrics. Through thorough experimentation, we have successfully validated the efficacy of our proposed method and have achieved outstanding results in predicting key weather parameters.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. Variations in the scalar potential and $S_3$ terms affect whether the standard model is normalized to zero or not, and whether a $Z_2$ symmetry is present, potentially identifying a dark matter candidate. The standard model is normalized by conditions on the scalar potential that eliminate brane effects, and a $Z_2$ symmetry is available in models where the standard model is normalized but not by the $S_3$ symmetry. The availability of a $Z_2$-protected model significantly increases when considering models where the standard model is normalized but not by the $S_3$ symmetry, and when allowing the mass of the dark matter candidate to deviate from the WMAP data, we find that there are twelve one-vev models and twenty-five two-vev models that could host dark matter.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target these disorders. This study contributes to the ongoing research in this area by using realistic three-dimensional simulations to investigate how neurons regulate transportation based on spatial demand. Our results show that a rapid and efficient delivery of materials can be achieved through an optimal combination of motor-based and microtubule-based transportation, depending on the distance to be traveled. This is accomplished by prioritizing the use of motor proteins for short-distance transport and switching to pure microtubule-based transportation for longer distances. Furthermore, the research finds that an anisotropic transport network can significantly improve the delivery of materials, especially for shorter distances. These findings provide insights into the existing transport mechanisms in neurons and highlight potential improvements to enhance material transportation.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The goal is to empower analysts to extract meaningful insights from data, thereby facilitating decision-making.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented in terms of the quantum numbers of the final hadronic state using the isobar model. Additionally, the work includes formulas for orbital angular momenta and the rules for describing the decay chains of arbitrary mass hadronic three-body systems, which also improves existing descriptions in terms of form factors.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. This parametrized space contains extreme points including $J_1 = J_{0.5,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{0,1}$, which corresponds to the variated Jaccard distance. Our analysis also discovered that the function $J_{\alpha,\beta}$ is equivalent to the $L_1$-norm for $\alpha$ equal to $0.5$ and $\beta$ equal to $1$.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning use paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we employ an innovative framework consisting of a dual deep network architecture that simultaneously deblurs images and estimates their blur kernel in a collaborative and efficient manner. This kernel is then used to form a blur matrix, which is further factorized into latent factors that minimize the impact of noise and improve the quality of the output. Our method's ability to process images at high speeds makes it suitable for processing videos in real-time. Our code and data are available for public access.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. In addition to the fundamental reaction system, the researchers propose more complex variations that incorporate enzymes and compartmentalised reactions to simulate biological systems, as well as a DNA-based system built upon the principle of DNA strand displacement. These innovative models offer promising avenues for exploring autonomous learning and potentially developing biological intelligent systems.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute.
